# litesearch


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

> Reading this on GitHub? The formatted
> [documentation](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/) is easier to
> read.

litesearch adds search to an application without a search server. Your
documents, their search indexes and their vectors live in one SQLite
file, and every query runs two kinds of search over them and merges the
results.

The first kind is keyword search. SQLite’s FTS5 extension keeps a
full-text index, which lists for every word the rows that contain it.
FTS5 ranks matching rows with bm25, a score that is higher when a row
contains the query’s words more often and when those words are rare in
the collection. Keyword search is exact. That is what you want for
names, error codes and identifiers, and it finds nothing when a document
says the same thing in different words.

The second kind is vector search. An encoder, also called an embedding
model, turns a piece of text into a list of a few hundred numbers called
an embedding. Texts with similar meanings get embeddings that are close
together. litesearch stores an embedding beside each piece of text,
embeds the query the same way, and returns the rows whose embeddings are
closest. Vector search finds “ending a membership” when the user typed
“cancel my subscription”, and it is weak at exact names.

Each kind of search returns a ranked list. litesearch merges the two
lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF): a row earns 1/(60 + its
position) from each list it appears in, and the amounts add up. A row
near the top of both lists beats a row at the top of only one. RRF uses
positions only, so it never has to compare a bm25 score with a vector
distance, and there is nothing to tune.

There are two ways to use the library.

Start with
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index). It is
built on
[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database),
and `Index.db` is the database underneath, so you can run a lower-level
query against the same data whenever
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) does
not do what you need.

## Install

``` python
# usearch's SQLite extension is fetched, probed and configured on first use (see litesearch.postfix)
!uv add litesearch
```

litesearch has no optional extras. Two features need a package that is
not installed with it: `rerank=True` needs `flashrank`, and the ONNX
encoder
[`FastEncode`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/utils.html#fastencode)
needs `onnxruntime`. Each is imported only when you use the feature, and
the error message names the package to install. `pip install litesearch`
installs everything else.

## Route 1: [`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index)

An [`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) is
a searchable collection. `add` puts files, folders or text into it. Each
document is cut into chunks, short passages of about 512 bytes, and each
chunk is stored with its embedding. `search` returns the chunks that
best match a query.

The other methods answer questions about whole documents and sections.
`sections` ranks sections instead of chunks, `read` returns the full
text of one section, `toc` lists everything in the index as a table of
contents, and `context` collects the best sections for a query in a form
you can pass to a language model.

``` python
ix = Index()                                        # pass a path to keep it on disk
ix.add('pdfs/attention_is_all_you_need.pdf')
hits = ix.search('how does multi-head attention work', limit=3)
[(h['heading'], h['page']) for h in hits]
```

Every hit has a `heading` and a `node_id`. While it ingests a document,
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) builds
a document tree from the document’s headings: the document is the root,
its chapters and sections are the nodes below, and each chunk records
the node it belongs to. `heading` is the path of headings above the
chunk, such as `attention is all you need › Abstract`, and `node_id`
names the section as the document’s id, `#`, and the section’s number. A
hit then tells you which section matched, which is what a reader or a
model needs, and not only which 512 bytes.

``` python
sec = ix.sections('how does multi-head attention work', limit=2)   # ranked *sections*, not chunks
[(s['node_id'], (s['snippets'] or [''])[0][:60]) for s in sec]
```

``` python
ix.read(sec[0]['node_id'])['text'][:300]            # one whole section, reassembled
```

``` python
ix.toc(summaries=False)                             # the corpus — no embeddings computed at all
```

One setting is left to you. `rerank=True` passes the top 30 candidates
to a cross-encoder from flashrank, a small model that reads the query
and each candidate together and scores how well they match. That is
slower than comparing embeddings and more accurate. In the evaluation it
improved weighted MRR by 0.026 to 0.077 and was positive in all twelve
measured cells. It makes a query roughly 10 times slower and downloads a
4 MB model the first time.

``` python
ix.search('how does multi-head attention work', rerank=True)
```

For source code, use `add_code`. It cuts Python files at top-level
functions and classes using Python’s own parser. Code chunks get no
document tree, so they have no `heading` or `node_id`, and `toc`,
`sections` and `read` do not cover them:

``` python
ix.add_code('litesearch')      # a directory, or the name of an installed package
```

## Route 2: [`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database)

[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database)
opens a SQLite database and returns a
[fastlite](https://fastlite.answer.ai/) `Database`. fastlite is a thin
layer over SQLite that gives each table a Python object. The first
vector search loads usearch’s SQLite extension into the connection,
which adds vector distance functions you can call from SQL.
`db.usearch_sql()` loads it before that, for SQL of your own. Pass a
file path to keep the database on disk, or nothing for one held in
memory.

``` python
db = database()
vecs = dict(v1=np.ones((100,), dtype=np.float32).tobytes(),
            v2=np.zeros((100,), dtype=np.float32).tobytes())
({m: db.q(f'select distance_{m}_f32(:v1,:v2) as d', vecs)[0]['d']
  for m in ['sqeuclidean', 'divergence', 'inner', 'cosine']}
 if db.usearch_sql() else 'usearch is off here, as on macOS 14')
```

There are four distance functions: `cosine`, `sqeuclidean` (squared
Euclidean distance), `inner` (one minus the dot product) and
`divergence` (Jensen-Shannon divergence). Each comes in four versions
for the number type the vectors are stored in: `f32`, `f16`, `f64` and
`i8`. Smaller results mean closer vectors.

The cell below does by hand what
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) does
for you. It loads an encoder, creates a store (a table with a text
column, an embedding column and a full-text index), embeds five
sentences, and searches them.

The comment in the middle points at the one mistake that is easy to
make. An embedding is stored as raw bytes, so a search has to be told
the number type the bytes hold. litesearch assumes float16, which uses
half the space of float32. The static encoder returns float32, so this
code converts to float16 before storing. If you store float32 and search
as float16, every distance comes back empty, litesearch prints a
warning, and the vector half of the search returns rows in table order.

``` python
enc   = static_embedder()             # model2vec: no GPU, no ONNX runtime
store = db.get_store(hash=True, ann=True)

# float16, because that is what a store holds. Handing it float32 fails quietly: every distance
# comes back 0 and the ranking degrades to keyword-only with no error.
emb   = lambda xs: np.asarray(enc.encode(list(xs)), dtype=np.float16)

texts = ['attention mechanisms in neural networks', 'transformer architecture for sequences',
         'stochastic gradient descent and learning rate schedules',
         'positional encoding and token embeddings', 'dropout reduces overfitting']
store.insert_all([dict(content=t, embedding=e.tobytes()) for t, e in zip(texts, emb(texts))],
                 upsert=True, hash_id='id', hash_id_columns=['content'])
store.rebuild_index()

q = 'self-attention mechanism'
db.search(q, emb([q])[0].tobytes(), columns=['content'], limit=2)
```

[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) exists
so that this setup is written once, correctly.

## Threads: share one connection, or give each thread its own

A SQLite connection used from several threads needs care.
`database(shared=True)` wraps the connection so that threads can share
it safely: each statement runs on its own, and a thread that opens a
transaction keeps the connection until it commits. The default
connection allows one thread at a time, so the alternative is to give
each thread its own
[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database)
on the same file. SQLite’s WAL mode, which litesearch turns on, lets
those connections read while another writes.

`python -m evals.shared_conn` measures both on a store of 20,000 rows
with an HNSW index, on a 14-core arm64 Mac:

The last column needs explaining. By default SQLite counts every memory
allocation under one lock shared by the whole process, so threads on
separate connections still wait for each other. Running
`apsw.shutdown(); apsw.config(apsw.SQLITE_CONFIG_MEMSTATUS, 0); apsw.initialize()`
before the first connection opens turns that counting off. After that,
`apsw.memory_used()` returns 0. litesearch does not do this for you,
because it changes the whole process.

Share one connection when your threads already share one database object
and writes are short. On a shared connection, a writer that commits
continuously makes readers wait a median of 106 ms. For parallel reads,
or a steady writer, give each thread its own connection and turn the
counting off. `evals/RESULTS.md` has the method and the results for
every thread count.

## What the evaluation says

The defaults come from `evals/`. It runs 120 known-item queries per
corpus over three corpora: EU legislation, arXiv papers and a
19th-century astrology treatise. A known-item query is one written to
find a specific passage. The queries come in five styles, from a copy of
the passage’s words to a paraphrase that shares none of them. The score
is MRR (mean reciprocal rank: 1 if the right section is first, 1/2 if
second, and so on, averaged over queries), counted per section and
weighted so that three quarters of the weight falls on queries that do
not copy the answer’s words. `python -m evals.decide` reproduces every
number.

The changes above the blank row are on by default. The ones below it are
off and stay off.

Three results matter more than any one row.

The choice of encoder matters little. Across `potion-32M`, `bge-small`,
`jina-v2-sm` and `egemma-300m` the spread is 0.018 to 0.046. The static
model, which looks up a vector per token instead of running a neural
network, wins one corpus outright and indexes about 1,700 times more
cheaply. The default is `potion-multilingual-128M`, a static model that
also covers scripts other than Latin.

The document tree does not improve ranking, and it is still worth
building. Ranking sections instead of chunks makes no difference.
Assembling them does: on a Sanskrit corpus, `context()` nearly doubles
verse-level recall over plain chunk search, from 0.190 to 0.340, the
largest single effect in `evals/`.

Keyword search alone beats the hybrid search on this benchmark, and the
benchmark is the reason. With
[`pre()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pre),
keyword-only search beats hybrid in all 24 paired cells, because every
query in the main set is a rewording of words from its target.
`evals/multihop.py` builds a second set where the answer shares no word
with the question. There keyword search cannot score at all, and the
vector search finds the target at rank 1 between 53% and 84% of the
time.

Three related jobs live in separate packages.
[pdflite](https://github.com/vedicreader/pdflite) reads PDFs.
[ganapati](https://github.com/vedicreader/ganapati) handles Sanskrit
metre, verse chunking and lemmas.
[vruksha](https://github.com/vedicreader/vruksha) builds an entity
graph; it measured negative for retrieval and `context` no longer calls
it (see `evals/RESULTS.md`).

Every store matches words across scripts, not only Sanskrit stores. A
tokenizer is the part of FTS5 that splits text into the words it
indexes. litesearch’s default tokenizer adds, beside each word, a copy
of it reduced to plain ASCII letters, so `श्रीमाता` (Devanagari),
`śrīmātā` (romanised with diacritics) and `srimata` all reach the same
row. It also adds a second, looser copy that follows English spelling
habits, so `Bheeshma` and `Bhishma` reach `भीष्म` and `Bhīṣma`. English
words keep their own entries, so nothing that matched before stops
matching. The looser copy makes the index 14.7% larger. This is the
largest retrieval gain measured here: a Devanagari query finds the right
verse every time (recall 1.000) with every encoder tested. The cost is
that a database built with this tokenizer cannot be searched by a
connection that has not registered it, which includes the plain
`sqlite3` command-line tool. Open it with
[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database).
